newsitem.title: USA: Bosnia vote could slow troop withdrawal.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia vote could slow troop withdrawal.

text.p: Municipal elections in Bosnia later this year could slow the withdrawal of peacekeeping troops, but they will be out within weeks after a Dec. 20 deadline, NATO's military chief insisted on Wednesday.

U.S. Army General George Joulwan, allied commander of NATO forces in Europe, refused at a Pentagon press conference to predict whether another international force would go to Bosnia next year after the current 58,000 NATO-led troops leave.
Secretary of State Warren Christopher hailed Bosnia's first national elections, but said the Clinton administration had not decided if U.S. troops should be sent there next year.

At a State Department news conference Christopher vowed that the United States, broker of the 1995 Dayton peace deal that led to the elections, would stay engaged in Bosnia and hold its leaders to their commitments to maintain a unified state.
Last weekend's successful polls meant that the NATO-led peace implementation force (IFOR) and its 15,000 member U.S. contingent could depart in December as planned, Christopher said.
He said the United States would press for municipal elections, which were delayed earlier, to be held this year. Joulwan said they could be held in November.

"We really have to take it one step at a time. People keep trying to drive us forward and anticipate questions that are not before us at the present time," said Christopher, stressing that U.S. and allied officials would discuss the subject of a possible follow-on force in the coming months.
"This is a very delicate time. We are getting into some bad weather ... with municipal elections coming up," Joulwan told reporters at the Pentagon.
He said he would insist that a "capable force" of IFOR troops remain in Bosnia to help provide security for those elections at some 4,500 polling stations.

"If there are going to be municipal elections before the end of our (Dec. 20) mandate, my recommendation would be that that drawdown would be limited" until the elections and then speeded up afterward, he said.
"I think we will have several weeks (after Dec. 20) before we get the force out," Joulwan added.
In Bosnia's national election, Bosnia's Moslem President Alija Izetbegovic narrowly defeated his Serb nationalist rival Momcilo Krajisnik to become first head of a new collective presidency.
The outcome was a relief to the United States because Izetbegovic supports a unified Bosnia. Many sceptics predicted the polls would never happen or be marred by violence.
The election "is a major victory for the democratic process ... The large turnout demonstrated that the Bosnian people were clearly determined to go to the polls," Christopher said.
